summary: This document updates RFC 768 (UDP) by describing where UDP options live, how they are written, and what they mean. The options go in spare space after the UDP data but before the end of the IP datagram.

eli5.summary: A parcel often has spare room in the box. UDP can now put little notes in that spare room without disturbing the main contents.

questions: how to add options to udp
how does udp fragmentation work with udp options
what is the udp surplus area

subtitle: How UDP gets room for header options, by using the spare bytes after the user data.

tldr.problem: TCP, SCTP and DCCP have space for transport options, but UDP's header has none, so features such as fragmentation or path MTU probing cannot be added cleanly.
tldr.mechanism: Because UDP has its own Length field, any bytes in the IP datagram after the UDP user data (the surplus area) can hold a checksum and a list of type-length-value options.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9868 updates RFC 768 to define that area and a set of options, designed so legacy receivers simply ignore them and still get the user data.

today: RFC 9868 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025. It updates RFC 768 and is not obsoleted by any later RFC. One use it describes, path MTU probing, is specified in RFC 9869.

sections.title: Why UDP Needs Options
sections.content:
Transport protocols grow by adding header options. TCP, the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) and the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) all have room for them, but RFC 768 (UDP) does not. RFC 9868 updates RFC 768 to give UDP transport options, with a generic syntax and meaning for a stateless, unreliable message protocol.

The trick is that UDP, unlike TCP, SCTP or DCCP, carries its own length field, separate from the IP length. The RFC says the real reason for that field is unknown, but it makes it possible to tell the UDP user data apart from whatever else the IP datagram carries. The RFC names uses such as fragmentation and reassembly, path MTU probing and, in future, authentication and encryption of the payload while still protecting the UDP header. Extensions do not apply to UDP-Lite.
sections.eli5: TCP has a place on its envelope for extra instructions, but UDP's envelope does not. This document finds a clever spot to write them anyway.

sections.title: The Surplus Area
sections.content:
Normally the UDP Length field and the size of the IP transport payload agree. When UDP Length is smaller, the leftover bytes after the UDP user data form the surplus area. RFC 9868 redefines the Length field as a "trailer options offset" and uses the surplus area for UDP Options. It can start at any byte offset, and it works even when the user data is empty (a UDP Length of 8), as long as there is room for the options.

The area starts with a 2-byte Option Checksum (OCS), aligned to the first 2-byte boundary relative to the start of the IP datagram, with zero bytes added before it if needed. The alignment bytes MUST be zero; if not, all options MUST be ignored and the surplus area silently discarded. The rest of the area is a list of options, which can end early with an End of Options List (EOL) option followed by zeros.

The same idea applies to IPv4 and IPv6. For IPv4 the bound is based on Total Length and IHL; for IPv6, on Payload Length minus extension headers.
sections.eli5: Imagine writing a letter that fits on half the page. The empty half is still part of the page, so you can use it for a note that readers who stop at the end of the letter never see.

sections.title: Checksum and Option Format
sections.content:
The OCS is an Internet checksum over the surplus area, including the surplus area's length. Its main job is to detect nonstandard uses of that area and accidental errors, not attacks. Computed this way, it also cancels the effect on the UDP checksum of errant middleboxes that wrongly cover the whole IP payload. The OCS MUST be non-zero when the UDP checksum is non-zero, and implementations MUST default to using it. If the OCS fails, all options MUST be ignored, but UDP user data validated by a correct UDP checksum is still delivered by default.

Each option starts with a one-byte Kind and a one-byte Length that counts the whole option. Only NOP and EOL are a single byte. A Length of 255 switches to an extended format with a 16-bit Extended Length. Options of 254 bytes or less MUST use the default format and options larger than 254 MUST use the extended one. Options are processed in the order they appear.
sections.eli5: Each note starts with a label saying what kind it is and how long it is, so the reader can skip a note it does not understand. A small check number at the front tells you if the whole notes area got smudged.

sections.title: The Defined Options
sections.content:
Kinds 0 to 191 are SAFE options: they can be ignored without changing the meaning of the user data. Kinds 192 to 255 are UNSAFE options, which may change or signal a change in the user data. Eight options are "must-support": EOL, NOP, APC, FRAG, MDS, MRDS, REQ and RES. All endpoints supporting UDP Options MUST recognize and be able to generate them. New options are not eligible for that status.

  • EOL (0) ends the list; all bytes after it MUST be zero. NOP (1) is a one-byte alignment pad, and packets SHOULD NOT use more than seven in a row.
  • APC (2) carries a 32-bit CRC32c of the user data, a stronger check than the UDP checksum. A failure is reported to the application but the data is still delivered.
  • MDS (4) hints at the largest datagram the sender of the option can receive without IP fragmentation. It MUST NOT be used to limit transmissions. MRDS (5) gives the largest reassembled datagram and how many fragments can be reassembled.
  • REQ (6) and RES (7) carry a 4-byte token. The upper layer decides whether and when to answer a REQ with a RES; UDP Options never do so automatically.
  • TIME (8) carries two 4-byte timestamps (TSval and TSecr) modeled on TCP timestamps, usable for round-trip time estimates. Zero is never a valid time value.
  • AUTH (9), UCMP (192) and UENC (193) are only reserved for future authentication, compression and encryption options. EXP (127) and UEXP (254) are for experiments, using a 16-bit experiment ID.

Other than FRAG, NOP, EXP and UEXP, an option SHOULD NOT appear more than once in a datagram. Receivers MUST interpret only the first instance. Must-support options other than NOP and EOL MUST come before other SAFE options. Unknown or malformed SAFE options are silently ignored.
sections.eli5: There is a menu of notes you can attach, such as a fingerprint of the message, a request for a reply, or a time stamp. A few are required of everyone, and the rest are optional extras. Some are only reserved for the future.

sections.title: Fragmentation and UNSAFE Options
sections.content:
The FRAG option (Kind 3) lets UDP split a message larger than the IP path allows into UDP fragments. Unlike IP fragments, every UDP fragment carries the same UDP ports, so it can pass stateless NATs. Each fragment has zero-length user data (UDP Length of 8); the fragment data sits in the surplus area after the options. Legacy receivers therefore see only empty UDP packets.

FRAG has two forms. The 10-byte form (Len=10) is for non-terminal fragments, and the 12-byte form (Len=12) marks the final fragment and adds a pointer (RDOS) to where the original datagram's options begin. A single unfragmented message may also use the 12-byte form with a Frag. Offset of zero. The 32-bit Identification field, together with the addresses and ports, identifies the original datagram and MUST be unique over the reassembly timeout.

Receivers MUST NOT let fragments overlap; if they do, reassembly is abandoned and no ICMP error is sent. The default reassembly timeout SHOULD be no more than 2 minutes, and expiry MUST NOT generate an ICMP error. Individual fragments MUST NOT be forwarded to the user. Endpoints MUST be able to handle at least two fragments, each fitting in a standard Ethernet MTU of 1,500 bytes.

UNSAFE options are only allowed inside fragments. Hiding the payload in the fragment area means a receiver that does not understand an UNSAFE option silently drops the data, instead of misreading it.
sections.eli5: If a parcel is too big for the mailbox, you cut it into labeled pieces, each in its own envelope with the same address. The receiver puts them back together. Anyone who does not know the trick just sees empty envelopes.

sections.title: Receiver Processing and the API
sections.content:
The design goal is that an options-aware receiver behaves like a legacy one unless told otherwise. If the UDP checksum fails, the packet is dropped. If it passes or is zero and the OCS fails, the user data is delivered and the options are ignored. If the OCS passes, the options are parsed and the user data is delivered whether or not each option is supported or succeeds. The sender decides which options to add; the receiver decides which to handle.

The API is extended so an application can require certain options on a receive port (packets lacking them MUST be silently dropped and SHOULD be logged), discard all packets with options, see the options received with each datagram, and choose options, a minimum datagram length and a maximum fragment size when sending. FRAG, NOP and EOL are not passed to the user. The default for dropping all packets with options MUST be to process them normally.

New options must follow rules: they MUST NOT be defined as must-implement, MUST NOT depend on the content of other options, MUST NOT declare their order relative to others, and MUST NOT be modified in transit. All options MUST say whether they can be used per fragment.
sections.eli5: By default the mail carrier still hands over your letter even if the little note on the back is smudged. Only if you tell the carrier a note is required will it refuse letters without a proper one.

sections.title: Legacy Devices and UDP-Lite
sections.content:
RFC 768 never forbade a UDP Length smaller than the IP payload. The RFC reports that no known systems use that gap for UDP, and says the OCS gives stronger protection against accidental matches than a static magic number. It states that UDP Options have been tested as interoperable with Linux, macOS and Windows Cygwin and worked through NAT devices; these systems delivered only the user data and silently discarded the surplus area.

It also notes caveats: one reported embedded device passes the entire IP datagram to the application, and the Alcatel-Lucent "Brick" Intrusion Detection System by default reports a mismatch between UDP and IP lengths as an attack, while other firewalls such as Check Point use a relaxed check by default. UDP-Lite cannot carry UDP Options because its Length field already marks the checksum coverage boundary. UDP Options also cannot work when UDP has no independent length, such as UDP Length of zero for IPv6 jumbograms, or when UDP is proxied over HTTP.
sections.eli5: Older mail machines should just read the letter and ignore the back of the page. The authors tried it on several common systems and it worked, though a few strict guards might mistake the extra space for a trick.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC compares UDP Options to TCP options: they add a control channel that can be abused if unprotected. DTLS does not protect the UDP header or the new options, just as TLS does not protect TCP options. Transport security is meant to come from the reserved AUTH and UENC options (when defined) or from IPsec. Options are visible on the path unless encrypted, and the RFC chose not to require encryption because the key infrastructure does not exist in many deployments.

Option parsing is serial, so an attacker could add many unknown options. Implementations SHOULD limit work on excessive or repeated options, and the rule that must-support options come first and appear once limits the impact. Of the must-support options, only REQ can make the upper layer send a response without user transmission. Implementations SHOULD limit pending fragments and reassembly space, and SHOULD NOT share reassembly limits across sockets. The RFC also notes that some middleboxes may strip options or drop such packets, in which case UDP Options do not function on that path.
sections.eli5: Notes on the back of a letter can be read by anyone handling it, and a prankster could stuff in lots of junk notes. So receivers are told to stay calm, set limits and not trust the notes unless they are properly sealed.
